hints: Think about where each ventricle sends blood. Which one pumps only to the nearby lungs, and which one pumps to the whole body?
Link thicker muscle to stronger contraction. What does the left side need to overcome in terms of pressure, resistance and distance that the right side does not?
walkthrough:
Compare the Two Destinations**
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood a short distance to the lungs in the pulmonary circuit. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood all around the body in the systemic circuit, a much longer distance with many more vessels.

Link Muscle Thickness to Pressure**
Thicker wall means more cardiac muscle, so a stronger contraction. The left ventricle needs this to generate high pressure to overcome the high resistance of the long systemic circuit. The right side only needs low pressure, which also protects the delicate lung capillaries from damage.

Final answer: Left ventricle generates higher blood pressure during systole to overcome higher resistance in the systemic circuit and to transport blood over a greater distance around the body than the right ventricle pumping to the lungs.

hints: Follow the black arrows for blood flow at stage K. Which vessels are bringing blood into the atria, and which vessel is leaving the right side near the top?
Remember that vessels are named by where they go, not by oxygen content. Which large vein returns body blood to the right atrium, and which artery leaves the right ventricle for the lungs?
walkthrough:
Identify F on the Right Side**
At K, the arrow in F shows blood flowing upwards into the right atrium from the body. This is the vena cava returning deoxygenated blood. The lower vessel shown is the inferior vena cava.

Identify G Leaving the Heart**
G is the large vessel leaving the upper part of the heart on the right side of the diagram. Blood from the right ventricle is pumped out through this vessel toward the lungs, so it is the pulmonary artery.
Final answer: F: (inferior / posterior) vena cava; G: pulmonary artery.

hints: Look at the arrows at K in Fig. 2.1. Blood is flowing from atria down into ventricles, but no blood is being ejected out of the ventricles. Are the chambers contracting or relaxing and filling?
walkthrough:
Read the Flow Pattern at K**
At K, blood flows into both atria and then down through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. The ventricles are not pumping out, they are relaxing and filling. This general relaxation and filling phase is diastole.

hints: Start with what you see at H and J. At H blood is moving up from ventricles to atria, at J blood is moving up out of the ventricles into the large arteries. What major contraction must happen in between?
Recall what triggers ventricular contraction after atrial systole. Where does the wave of excitation go after the atrioventricular node?
Think about pressure. When ventricles contract, how does ventricular pressure change relative to atrial pressure first, and what does that do to the AV valves?
Next, compare ventricular pressure to pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery. What must happen for the semilunar valves to open?
Finish the sequence by stating where blood goes and what the atria are doing at the same time.
walkthrough:
Excitation Spreads to the Ventricles**
After the atria have contracted, a wave of excitation passes from the atrioventricular node down the Bundle of His and Purkyne fibres to the base of the ventricles. This ensures a coordinated contraction.

Ventricular Systole Begins From the Base**
Both ventricles contract together, starting at the base and squeezing upwards. This pushes blood up toward the large arteries rather than trapping it at the bottom.

Rising Pressure Closes the AV Valves**
As the ventricular muscle contracts, blood pressure in the ventricles rises. When it becomes greater than pressure in the atria, the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) are forced shut. This prevents backflow into the atria, which you can see has stopped by stage J.

Higher Pressure Opens the Semilunar Valves**
Pressure keeps rising until ventricular pressure is greater than pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery. The semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves then open and blood is forced out of the ventricles.

Blood Ejected While Atria Refill**
Blood flows into the aorta to the body and into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs, as shown by the upward arrows at J. At the same time the atria are relaxing in atrial diastole and filling with incoming blood from the veins and pulmonary veins.

Final answer: Wave of excitation from AVN passes down Bundle of His / Purkyne fibres; both ventricles contract from base upwards (ventricular systole); ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure closing AV valves; ventricular pressure rises above artery pressure opening semilunar valves; blood ejected into aorta and pulmonary artery to body and lungs, while atria are in diastole and refilling.
